fields.current: From January 1, 2027, new, increased or extended local special taxes put on the ballot by citizen petition need two-thirds approval, the same bar as those placed by city councils and boards. Per the measure text, it applies only to special taxes, not general taxes. It was placed on the ballot in a deal that kept a broader anti-tax initiative off it.

evidence.excerpt: Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government,
including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase
government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property,
except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D.
General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise.

fields.explanation: The two-thirds rule, date and scope are supported. 'Applies only to special taxes' is incomplete: Sec. 4.5(b) separately bars ad valorem real property taxes by initiative, beyond what Art. XIII D already allows. The text has no general-tax language. The ballot deal is reported only by independent sources (CalMatters, Hoover, Burke Williams & Sorensen), so it should be attributed.
fields.proposedText: From January 1, 2027, new, increased or extended local special taxes need two-thirds voter approval even when citizens put them on the ballot, the same bar as those placed by city councils and boards. General taxes are not covered. It also bars citizen initiatives from adding local property taxes beyond what the constitution already allows. News reports say it came from a deal that kept a broader anti-tax initiative off the ballot.
fields.limitations: The meaning of the Art. XIII D cross-reference in 4.5(b) was not confirmed by an official source; Hoover describes it as the existing 1 percent limit.

specificGaps: Confirm Sonoma County 2024 half-cent sales tax result (62%) and whether it was citizen-initiated, from the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters.
Gov. Newsom and CSAC listed as opponents with no source found; a law firm summary says the measure was a compromise involving Newsom's office.
The ballot deal (HJTA initiative withdrawn) is reported only by independent sources; Hoover names AG No. 25-0006A1 but we did not read an SOS withdrawal record.
The meaning of the Art. XIII D Sec. 3(a)(1) exception in Sec. 4.5(b) was not confirmed by an official source.
conflicts: Props 41 and 42 conflict clauses reach only 'another initiative measure'. Prop 43 is a legislative constitutional amendment, so on the text it is not caught by them.

Our 'con' lists Gov. Newsom as an opponent; Burke, Williams & Sorensen describes Prop 43 as 'a compromise between Governor Newsom's office and the proponents'. Not a direct contradiction, but no source confirms opposition.
Hoover and CalMatters say Assemblymember Buffy Wicks authored ACA 22 and now opposes it.
